chapter_theme: Manimekalai wakes the king of Savakam, Aputhiran reborn, to his former birth: he hears his birth story, resolves to renounce, is argued back to his duty by his minister, sails to Manipallavam where the dharma seat shows him his past, and is shown by the island's goddess the bones of his former body and of those who died following his fast; the goddess tells Manimekalai how Puhar was cursed into the sea, and Manimekalai sends the king home to rule, telling him a king's dharma is food, clothing and shelter for all lives.

cast.role: the bowl's first owner, reborn from a cow's womb as king of Savakam (Punyarajan); called அரசன், இறைவன், மன்னவன் in this kaathai
Madhavi's daughter, who now holds the bowl and has come to Savakam
the Buddhist teacher in the grove of Savakam from whom the king hears dharma
the king's chamberlain, who had sailed to Puhar and heard of Manimekalai there
the sage on the bank of the Kayankarai whose sermon Manimekalai recalls from her former birth
the all-knowing one whose coming the sage foretold and for whom the seat was made
Indra, king of the gods, who set the dharma seat on Manipallavam
the childless king of Savakam who raised Aputhiran as his son
the queen of Savakam, the king's foster mother, who tells him of his birth
the minister of Savakam who argues against the king's renunciation
the goddess of the temple of learning in Madurai who gave Aputhiran the bowl, addressed here as the image of the arts of Madurai
the guardian goddess of Manipallavam, here called காவல் தெய்வதம்
daughter of the king of the Naga land, mother of the Chola king's infant son
the merchant whose ship takes the infant prince and is wrecked
the Chola king of Puhar, Udayakumaran's father, who loses his infant son and neglects the Indra festival
the sea goddess who curses Puhar to be swallowed by the sea
the Buddhist teacher, who leaves the drowning city for Vanji with Manimekalai's mothers
Manimekalai's mother
Manimekalai's companion, counted among her mothers
the nine merchants of Aputhiran's ship who came back for him and died where he had died

manimekalai:25:1-24.reading: The king of Savakam enters the grove with his household, worships the teacher Dharmasavakan and hears from him dharma and its opposite, the impermanent and the permanent, suffering, the passage of lives, dependent arising and release by cutting it; seeing a peerless woman with a bowl in her hand listening to dharma, he asks who she is, the chamberlain tells him she is the girl whose birth Aravanan revealed in Puhar, and Manimekalai tells the king that his bowl has come into her hand and asks what he has done, bewildered by wealth, not knowing even this birth of his from a cow's womb.
manimekalai:25:1-24.nuance: The teaching the king hears (3 to 6) is a list of Buddhist headings, ending with dependent arising and release by cutting it (சார்பு அறுத்து உய்தி), but it has not woken him; it takes Manimekalai's reproach to do that. Her charge is not that he has forgotten a former life, which few remember, but that wealth has hidden from him even the present one (23 to 24), the cow's womb he was born from.
manimekalai:25:1-24.event: The king of Savakam hears dharma from Dharmasavakan, asks who the woman with the bowl is, and Manimekalai tells him his bowl is now in her hand and reproaches him for not knowing his birth.

claims.claim: one is saved by cutting the chain of dependent arising

manimekalai:25:25-41.reading: Manimekalai tells the king he will not know the nature of bound birth unless he circles Manipallavam and bids him come there, then rises into the clear sky, comes down before sunset on the island's flowered shore, circles it, sees the jewelled seat of the bond-free great ascetic and, as she worships and circles it, the seat's flawless sight makes her know her birth again, and she begins to speak of how on the Kayankarai bank she bowed to the sage, heard dharma and praised him.
manimekalai:25:25-41.event: Manimekalai summons the king to Manipallavam, flies there herself, circles the dharma seat and recalls again her former birth.

manimekalai:25:42-63.reading: Manimekalai, speaking as if to the sage of her former birth, recalls his proclamation to all who went with him: put away the evil deeds that make men beasts, hell-beings and ghosts, and you become gods, men and Brahmas, so keep up good deeds unwearied; an all-knowing one will appear to save the world, and none but those who hear his dharma escape painful birth, so practise dharma before death comes; and she recalls that after his harsh word to her she asked why the seat had been placed before the Great One's coming and why it shows her birth, and he answered that it bears none but the all-knowing first one, that the god will not worship it until it has borne him, and that the god set it for him and bade it declare the births of those born.
manimekalai:25:42-63.nuance: The 'harsh word' (வெவ் உரை, 53) is the sage's prophecy in kaathai 9 that Rahulan would die within sixteen days and she would enter his pyre; here she places in the same hearing her question about the seat, so the seat's power was explained to her in the life she lost. Good deeds earn better births (43 to 44), but only hearing the coming Buddha's dharma ends birth (47 to 48): the sermon keeps those two apart. Who கரியவன் (55) is, who placed the seat, is not clear; at 182 the seat is said to have been set by the king of the gods. Lines 56 to 57 (மன் பெரும் பீடிகை மாய்ந்து உயிர் நீங்கிய என் பிறப்பு) are hard to construe.
manimekalai:25:42-63.event: Manimekalai recalls the sage's sermon on deeds and rebirth and his explanation of why the dharma seat reveals births.

claims.claim: evil deeds lead to birth as beasts, hell-beings and ghosts, and avoiding them leads to birth as gods, men and Brahmas
none escape painful birth except those who hear the dharma of the all-knowing one who is to come
dharma must be practised before death, which cannot be turned back, arrives

manimekalai:25:64-76.reading: The sage's answer ends: because the god so ordained, the seat will show her births too, clearing the dark; Manimekalai says the word the sage spoke that day has come true for her today, praises and circles the seat; meanwhile the king leaves the grove for the inner city and learns of the birth in which a sage was his father and a cow his mother, how by the sage's grace he lay in a golden egg without the cord of the gut, and how childless Bhumichandran took him, hearing it from his mother Amarasundari.
manimekalai:25:64-76.nuance: The king learns his former birth twice: from his foster mother in the palace (70 to 77) before the seat shows it to him (134 to 138). The golden egg 'not wound in the gut-chain' (72 to 73) marks this birth as unsoiled by the womb.
manimekalai:25:64-76.event: Manimekalai says the sage's word is fulfilled; the king returns to the city and hears from his mother the story of his birth from a cow and his adoption.

manimekalai:25:77-95.reading: Grieving at what he hears, the king thinks of what his mother did in the life he lost and of the nature of the birth he now has, and declares that it is good to renounce wholly the intoxicating game of desire that kingship is, with its throne before which kings wait, its dancing and music, its waiting on queens' sulks, painting saffron on their breasts and drinking their smiles under the sugarcane bow's arrows; the seed the clear-sighted lord sowed in his ear, he says, has ripened today without fault, with Manimekalai as its cause.
manimekalai:25:77-95.nuance: 'What the mother did' (78) is the abandonment of the newborn Aputhiran by Saali in his former birth. The king does not renounce kingship as a burden but as a drunkenness of pleasure (காமக் கள்ளாட்டு, 91): his catalogue is the life of a pleasure-king, not of a protector. The 'clear lord' who sowed the seed (93) is most likely Dharmasavakan, whose teaching he had just heard in the grove. His claim is answered: the minister calls it a wrong judgment by the Buddha's own example (115 to 118), and Manimekalai sends him back to rule with the dharma of grace (226 to 231).
manimekalai:25:77-95.event: Hearing his birth story, the king grieves and declares he will give up kingship and its pleasures for renunciation.

claims.claim: a king does well to give up kingship and its pleasures wholly for renunciation

manimekalai:25:96-114.reading: Seeing the king's mind changed, the minister Janamitran bows and tells him that before his father had him, this land had no rain for twelve years, so that creatures died and a mother would eat alone without pity for her infant; he appeared like a raincloud in a burning summer, and since then the sky has not failed nor the earth its yield, and no creature has known hunger; if he goes, his land will cry like an infant whose mother is gone, and if he seeks the higher world without guarding this suffering one, then even as lives perish, lord,
manimekalai:25:96-114.nuance: The minister ties the rain not to the king's rule but to his birth (105 to 109): the merit that returns the rain is Aputhiran's giving in his former life, carried into this one (kaathai 14, 95 to 104). The mother eating alone in the famine (103 to 104) is the reversal of the bowl's ethic of feeding others first. The unit ends mid-sentence; the minister's argument completes at 115 to 118.
manimekalai:25:96-114.event: The minister Janamitran tells the king of the twelve-year famine that ended at his birth and warns that his land will be orphaned if he leaves.

claims.claim: the birth of a meritorious king brings back the rain and ends hunger

manimekalai:25:115-139.reading: you would gain what you desire, the minister says, yet the dharma of the Buddha, first of all lives, who does not pity his own life and protects the lives of others, is not this, and the king has judged wrongly; the king answers that the unquenchable longing to circle Manipallavam is hard to quiet, charges the minister to guard kingdom, queens and city for one month, summons shipwrights, sails, and reaches the island, where Manimekalai, glad to see the king's ship, circles it with him and shows him the dharma seat, which, as he circles and praises it, shows him his ended birth like a clear mirror held to a face, and he cries that he knows his birth and his grief is ended, hailing the image of the arts of Tamil Madurai.
manimekalai:25:115-139.nuance: The minister turns the Buddha's own example against the king's renunciation: the Buddha's mark is that he does not pity his own life (116 to 117), and seeking a higher world for oneself while one's people suffer is pity for oneself. The king does not answer the argument; he asks only for a month to circle the island. Line 118 ஒர்ந்தனை is read as ஓர்ந்தனை.
manimekalai:25:115-139.event: The minister appeals to the Buddha's example; the king leaves him to guard the realm for a month, sails to Manipallavam, and the dharma seat shows him his former birth.

claims.claim: the Buddha's dharma, which pities not one's own life and protects the lives of others, does not leave a suffering world to seek a higher world for oneself

manimekalai:25:140-150.reading: The king recalls to the goddess of Madurai how, when hungry beggars came to him in the rest hall in the middle of a rainy night and he grieved with no food to give, she put Amudasurabi in his palm saying the bowl would not fail though the land did, and so cut off his round of becoming; he hails her, who rises in the mind and makes the meaning of words known, and begins to praise her feet, which even gods and Brahmas worship.
manimekalai:25:140-150.nuance: The goddess's words at 144 to 145 repeat almost word for word those Aravanar gave her in kaathai 14 (12 to 13): the king's own memory now agrees with the teacher's account. பவம் அறுவித்த (147) is read as 'who cut off my becoming'; it may mean only that she ended his misery.
manimekalai:25:140-150.event: The king, knowing his former birth, recalls and praises Chintadevi's gift of the bowl.

manimekalai:25:151-174.reading: Praising her feet, which wash the stain of the tongue, the king vows never to forget them in any birth, then goes with Manimekalai southwest to the Gomukhi pool and sits in the shade of a punnai; the island's guardian goddess, glad to see Aputhiran there, comes and tells him: you who held in your palm the medicine that saves life and ended great suffering, you have come; those who forgot you that day came back later, saw what you had done and gave up their lives where you had lain: see the bones of the nine merchants and of those who ate from their hands and died grieving; see your own bony frame under the sand by the punnai; you killed your own life, and, pitying your life, the others who came later killed theirs: are you not a killer? you have become a king.
manimekalai:25:151-174.nuance: The goddess's charge reckons self-starvation as killing (நின் உயிர் கொன்றாய், 172) and lays the later deaths of the merchants and their company on Aputhiran, who set the example; then she turns the charge with a play of sound, கொலைவன் against கொற்றவன் (174): the 'killer' has become a king. Whether this is reproach or wonder is not settled by the Tamil. Line 170 (அன்பு உடை ஆர் உயிர் அரசற்கு அருளிய) is hard: read as the body that, by the loving life it gave up, gave the king his kingship.
manimekalai:25:151-174.event: At the Gomukhi pool the island's guardian goddess shows the king the bones of the nine merchants who died where he had died and calls him a killer who has become a king.

claims.claim: giving up one's own life by fasting is killing, and the one who does it bears the deaths of those who follow him

manimekalai:25:175-199.reading: Turning to Manimekalai, the goddess tells her why her great city went into the sea: Pilivalai, daughter of the Naga king, came with her newborn son by the Chola of the sun's line, circled the island and the seat Indra set, and gave the boy to the merchant Kambalan, whose ship had put in, as the king's son; he took the child with joy, but that night the ship was wrecked on the shore and the boy lost; the Chola, told of it, searched beach, sea and shore like a cobra that has lost its gem, the city's Indra festival lapsed, and the goddess Manimekala, unable to bear that, cried 'let the sea take the city'.
manimekalai:25:175-199.nuance: The city's ruin has a chain of causes with no evil intent in it: a mother's gift, a shipwreck, a father's grief, a festival forgotten in that grief, and a goddess's anger at the lapse. The king's search 'like a cobra that has lost its gem' (195) recalls the Naga line of the lost child.
manimekalai:25:175-199.event: The guardian goddess tells how the Chola's infant son by Pilivalai was lost in a shipwreck, the grieving king neglected the Indra festival, and Manimekala cursed Puhar to be taken by the sea.

manimekalai:25:200-221.reading: The goddess ends: the curse was laid and came to pass; as the waves swallowed the city, its king went off alone like Indra leaving his drowned city, and the sage went safely with Manimekalai's mothers to Vanji; if she would hear how Manimekala once rescued her lord of all lives from the sea and how he then ruled as a king of dharma, she will hear it from Aravanan in Vanji; the goddess departs, and the king, grieving, digs the sand with Manimekalai and uncovers his former body, the flesh fallen away but the bones still holding together, seated as if coated in white lime, and the king is bewildered at the sight until Manimekalai rises and asks him what has befallen him.
manimekalai:25:200-221.nuance: The skeleton is kept whole (216 to 217): the flesh's bonds have loosened but the bones' have not, and it sits in the posture of the faster as if plastered for a shrine. The sight that might teach the body's impermanence instead bewilders the king (220). Lines 207 to 212 are compressed: 'the guardian of the wide sea' (207) is read as Manimekala, and 'your lord of lives' (209) as the Buddha in a former birth whom she saved from the sea.
manimekalai:25:200-221.event: The goddess tells of Puhar's drowning and the flight of Manimekalai's mothers to Vanji and departs; the king digs up his own former skeleton and is bewildered.

manimekalai:25:222-239.reading: Manimekalai tells the king that she came to his land and called him here to show him his former birth so that his name would stand on this island and on the great continent; if kings who rule the wide earth take up the dharma of grace, nothing else is needed to remove faults, and if he asks what dharma is, he should remember that for all living beings it is nothing but food, clothing and shelter; the king vows to do this good dharma in his own land and in others', says she has made him anew by revealing his birth and that he cannot bear to part from her, and she bids him not grieve, for his land calls him back, to go by ship while she goes to Vanji, and rises into the sky.
manimekalai:25:222-239.nuance: Manimekalai does not take the king's offered renunciation; she sends him back to rule and defines his dharma as material provision for every life (230), the bowl's work made a king's duty. His reply widens it at once beyond his own kingdom (232). The kaathai ends on என் running into the next.
manimekalai:25:222-239.event: Manimekalai tells the king that a king's dharma is food, clothing and shelter for all, he vows to practise it, and she sends him home by ship and flies to Vanji.

claims.claim: if kings take up the dharma of grace, nothing else is needed to remove the world's faults
dharma for all living beings is nothing but food, clothing and shelter

links.note: Aravana Adigal told Manimekalai that Aputhiran died with an unquenched purpose of sustaining lives and was born from a cow's womb to rule Savakam; here Manimekalai tells that king that, bewildered by wealth, he knows neither that birth nor the cow's womb of this one.
links.teaches: Rebirth carried Aputhiran's purpose into a king's body but not his knowledge of it, so the purpose has to be handed back to him by one who heard his story from outside.

links.note: Kural 335 urges good deeds before the hiccup stops the tongue; the sage of Kayankarai urges dharma before death that cannot be turned back (49 to 50), but adds that good deeds win only better births and that none escape birth except those who hear the coming Buddha.
links.teaches: The sermon separates what the couplet joins: haste in good deeds before death decides the next birth, but release waits on a teacher not yet come, so urgency to do good is not urgency to be free.

gains.a: a measure of what is shared Tamil ethics in the sermon, so that only its claim at 47 to 48 stands out as Buddhist doctrine
gains.b: a limit the couplet does not state: good deeds rushed to before death lead on to heaven or a human birth but do not end birth

links.note: In kaathai 9 the sage foretold that on the island seat she would know her birth and find his word clear; at her second visit Manimekalai says the sage's word of that day has come true today, after recalling his account of why the seat reveals births.
links.teaches: The second visit adds the ground of the seat's power, Indra's order made for the coming Buddha, so the fulfilment rests on the Buddha's future presence and not on the seat itself.

links.note: The king declares it good to renounce kingship wholly, crediting Manimekalai as the cause; Manimekalai, whose call woke him, sends him back to rule and tells him a king's dharma is food, clothing and shelter for all.
links.teaches: The epic of renunciation turns its heroine against a king's renunciation: the waking she causes is meant to make him a giver on a throne, not an ascetic, so renunciation is not the right end for everyone it moves.

links.note: Kural 545 says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who wields the sceptre rightly; the minister says rain returned to Savakam after twelve years when the king was born, before he wielded any sceptre.
links.teaches: The epic moves the cause of a land's plenty from the king's rule to his birth, that is, to merit carried from a former life of giving, so a king can bring rain before he governs at all.

gains.a: a Tamil rule that makes the minister's report a claim about kingship rather than a bare wonder
gains.b: a case its link between rain and right rule cannot explain: rain that follows a king's coming and precedes his rule

links.note: Puram 186 says the world lives not by rice or water but by its king, who must know he is its life; the minister tells the king that if he leaves, his land will cry like an infant whose mother is gone (110 to 111).
links.teaches: The Sangam duty that a king know himself the world's life becomes, in a Buddhist epic, the argument that holds a king back from renunciation, so the poem's maxim sets a limit even on seeking release.

gains.a: a Sangam warrant that makes the minister's plea a statement of a king's duty rather than a courtier's flattery
gains.b: an application the poem does not foresee: the king's being the world's life binds him against leaving it for a higher world

links.note: Kural 244 says one who sustains lives (மன்னுயிர் ஓம்பி) and holds to grace need fear no deed for his own life; the minister says the Buddha's dharma is not to pity one's own life and to protect other lives (பிற உயிர் ஓம்பும், 116), and charges the king with seeking a higher world for himself.
links.teaches: The couplet promises the protector of lives safety for his own; the minister makes indifference to one's own life the protector's mark, so a king's wish for his own release counts against his grace.

gains.a: a Tamil rule that makes protecting others' lives the core of grace, so the minister's appeal reads as more than Buddhist piety
gains.b: a reversal of its reward: in the epic the protector of lives is the one who does not seek safety for himself, not the one granted it

links.note: Aravana Adigal told Manimekalai that Chintadevi gave Aputhiran the bowl on a rainy night saying it would not fail though the land did; the reborn king, his birth shown him by the seat, recalls the same night and the goddess's words almost word for word.
links.teaches: The teacher's story and the seat's revelation agree to the word, so the king's restored memory works in the epic as proof that the seat shows births truly.

links.note: Kural 327 says not to take another's life even at the cost of one's own; the island goddess tells Aputhiran that by starving he killed his own life and that the merchants who came back and died where he lay died for his sake, so that he is a killer.
links.teaches: The couplet treats giving up one's own life as a price that may be paid to avoid killing; the epic counts giving up one's own life as itself a killing, and one that draws others to die.

gains.a: a known Tamil rule against which the goddess's charge reads as a judgment about killing, not only grief for the dead
gains.b: a case its two lives cannot keep apart: one's own death that becomes the cause of others' deaths

links.note: Aravana Adigal told Aputhiran's death by fasting as a sun that sets in the west to rise again, with an unquenched purpose of sustaining lives; the island goddess calls the same death a killing of his own life that led others to kill theirs.
links.teaches: The epic gives two endorsed voices opposite verdicts on one death, the teacher's passage to a sustaining birth and the guardian's charge of killing, and leaves both standing beside the king who is its fruit.

links.note: Pathirakiriyar asks when he will see the bones within as white bones and himself lowered like a cast-off corpse; the king digs up his own former body, bones held together as if coated in white lime, and is bewildered.
links.teaches: The epic grants literally the sight the Siddhar longs for, one's own body as white bones, and shows that the sight alone does not free: the king is bewildered until Manimekalai tells him what it is for.

gains.a: a frame in which seeing one's own corpse is a discipline of release, against which the king's bewilderment is a failure to read it
gains.b: a test of its longing: the sight given in full, without the knowledge that would make it freeing

links.note: Puram 189 measures every man's need, king or hunter, by one measure of food and two cloths and concludes that wealth's use is giving; Manimekalai tells the king that dharma for all lives is nothing but food, clothing and shelter.
links.teaches: The Sangam measure of human need, used to tell a rich man to give, becomes the entire content of a king's dharma toward every life, and the king at once extends it to other kingdoms.

gains.a: a Sangam ground for reducing dharma to three material needs, so the definition reads as a measure of need and not a slight on doctrine
gains.b: a widening of its argument: what each person needs becomes what a king owes all lives, in his land and in others'

new_concepts.gloss: the vow of not eating: giving up life by fasting
new_concepts.label_source: label from kaathai 14 (உண்ணா நோன்போடு, 14:95); this kaathai describes the death without the word

new_concepts.gloss: a curse, a word spoken in grief or anger that binds its object and comes to fruit, even in a later birth
the festival; a public feast of a god or a town
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word (line 197, விழாக் கோள்)

source_issues: Line 31 had a leftover HTML quote mark, removed in the core file.
Line 93 தெளிந்த was repaired from an old-font ௌ.

Line 37 opens a quotation inside Manimekalai's speech that runs to line 67 with further nested quotations (41-50, 54-57, 58-65); the nesting is hard to follow and the speaker of 54-57 (Manimekalai in her former birth) is inferred.
Lines 55-57: கரியவன் as the one who placed the seat is unclear (line 182 says the king of the gods set it), and மன் பெரும் பீடிகை மாய்ந்து உயிர் நீங்கிய is hard to construe.
Line 170 அன்பு உடை ஆர் உயிர் அரசற்கு அருளிய is obscure.
Lines 207-212 are compressed and the referents of 'the guardian of the sea' and 'your lord of lives' are inferred.
The kaathai ends on என் (239), running into kaathai 26; the last unit has break score 0.
